world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Heath, Jeffrey (1980). Dhuwal (Arnhem Land) texts on kinship and other subjects, with grammatical sketch and dictionary. Oceania Linguistics Monographs 23. (Gumatj is a Dhuwal/Dhuwala dialect.)

new_statements.quote: e) Stress: Stress is almost always on the first syllable of a word but there are a few exceptions. Long vowels only occur in stressed syllables. [Scope stated p.33: 'For Eastern Dhuwal/Dhuwala dialects and probably for most if not all languages at Yirrkala ...'; p.31: 'Djapu and Gumatj in particular are taken as points of reference'.] || Morphy 1983 (Djapu), p.25: '2.2.7 STRESS, VOWEL LENGTH AND CONSONANT GEMINATION. Stress in Djapu is predictable: it almost always occurs on the first syllable of a word. Schebeck (personal communication) points out that the handful of exceptions to the general rule are predominantly words in which the second syllable begins with /d/, for example budapthu-N "go down and cross" and bandany "dry, clear".'
new_statements.citation: Amery, Rob. 1985. A new diglossia: contemporary speech varieties at Yirrkala in North East Arnhem Land. MA thesis, Australian National University. Chapter 2 'Phonology', sec. 2.1 'Summary of Yolngu Matha phonology', Phonotactics (e) Stress.
new_statements.locator: p.36 (PDF p.52), sec. 2.1, 'Phonotactics... e) Stress'; cf. Morphy 1983 Djapu sec. 2.2.7 p.25 (PDF p.49 of)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (extracted text, PDF p.52 = thesis p.36). Under 'Phonotactics... e) Stress:' the text reads exactly: 'Stress is almost always on the first syllable of a word but there are a few exceptions. Long vowels only occur in stressed syllables.' (text layer has scanned letter-spacing 'fir s t' only). The scope framing the reader cites is also there verbatim: p.31 (PDF p.47) 'Djapu and Gumatj in particular are taken as points of reference because they are the main patrilects... and have been best described by linguists (Morphy, 1983 for Djapu and Ross, 1968 etc. for Gumatj). Gumatj is also the official vernacular language of the Yirrkala Community School bilingual program. Gumatj and Djapu are…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress falls on the first syllable of the word (the only syllable that may host a long vowel); a small closed set of lexical exceptions has non-initial stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Amery says nothing. For Yolngu generally, Wood 1978 (Gaalpu) assigns weaker stresses to the first syllable of each following 2-3-syllable stress group, restarting after root boundaries in compounds/reduplications; Morphy 1983 (Djapu, sec. 2.3 headnote in TOC) and Wilkinson 2012 (Djambarrpuyngu) follow similar stress-group accounts; Jepson 2019 finds no acoustic evidence for secondary stress in Djambarrpuyngu.
new_statements.exceptions: 'a few exceptions' (Amery, unspecified); Morphy/Schebeck for Djapu: mostly words whose second syllable begins with the apico-domal flap, e.g. budapthu- 'go down and cross', bandany 'dry, clear'; Wood (Gaalpu): some pronominals and place names (pu'ralku, pur'wu).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement (phonotactics of the word); long vowels restricted to the initial = stressed syllable. Statement is framed for Yolngu Matha at Yirrkala (Gumatj, Djapu, Dhuwaya) rather than for Gumatj alone.
new_statements.identity_note: No Gumatj-only phonological description was found online. The quoted statement (Amery 1985) sits in a 'Summary of Yolngu Matha phonology' inside an MA thesis on Dhuwaya ('Baby Gumatj', the Yirrkala koine), which takes Gumatj and Djapu as its reference patrilects and says the phonology holds 'for Eastern Dhuwal/Dhuwala dialects and probably for most if not all languages at Yirrkala'; its wording closely follows Morphy 1983 on Djapu (djap1238, a Dhuwal dialect; Glottolog groups Gumatj guma1253 with Dhuwal dhuw1249 under 'Western Dhuwal-Dhuwala' west2439). Morphy 1983 (Djapu, p.25) is the fuller published sibling statement and is also saved. Gumatj-specific primary description exists only as Joyce Ross's unpublished typescripts (1968, 1971, 1975).

sources.note: Ch.2 'Summary of Yolngu Matha phonology' (reference patrilects Gumatj and Djapu; Dhuwaya), p.36: 'Stress is almost always on the first syllable of a word but there are a few exceptions. Long vowels only occur in stressed syllables.' Also notes Yirrkala intonation is comparatively level vs the 'sing-song' pattern of Milingimbi/Galiwin'ku.

sources.citation: Jepson, Kathleen. 2019. The prosody of Djambarrpuyngu... PhD thesis, University of Melbourne.
sources.note: Sec. 1.2.2.5 reviews Wilkinson 2012 p.62 ('stress patterning in Djambarrpuyngu is largely predictable', initial primary stress; secondary by Wood/Waters stress groups); her acoustic study finds initial prominence cued mainly by pitch and no evidence for secondary stress. Mentions Gumatj only re stop phonetics (Butcher 2006).

sources.citation: Morphy, Frances. 1983. Djapu, a Yolngu dialect. In R.M.W. Dixon & B.J. Blake (eds), Handbook of Australian Languages vol. 3, 1-188. Canberra: ANU Press.
sources.note: Djapu (Dhuwal sibling of Gumatj), sec. 2.2.7 p.25: stress predictable, almost always on the first syllable; handful of exceptions mostly words whose second syllable begins with the flap /d/ (budapthu-N, bandany); long vowels only in initial syllables; consonant after a short-vowel open initial syllable often geminated (initial stressed syllables tend to be heavy). p.1: 'Stress is predictable, with primary stress occurring on the first syllable of a word.'

sources.note: Grepped full text: no section on word stress; only incidental remarks (unstressed enclitics/particles, 'full word-stress on the long vowel' of an interjection, contrastive stress not used as in English). Dhuwal (Djapu etc.), not Gumatj.

sources.citation: Wood, Ray. 1978. Some Yuulngu phonological patterns. In Papers in Australian Linguistics 11, 53-117. Pacific Linguistics A-51.
sources.note: Gaalpu (Dhangu) with remarks on Yuulngu generally, sec. 3 'The stress group' (pp.85-87): stress predictable; words consist of 2-3-syllable stress groups whose initial syllable is stressed; word-initial syllable carries primary stress; later groups subordinate (secondary); pattern restarts after root boundary in reduplicated/compound stems; a few exceptions (mainly pronominals, some place names with second-syllable stress).
